reading.body:
Retail AI is tracked by four independent sources covering adoption, store technology, market size, and software spend, but none of them measures the compute or power behind those systems.

The four sources form a layered measurement stack. Census BTOS updates adoption every two weeks across all sectors, including retail trade. NRF adds detail on store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software. Coresight sizes the market for merchandising and supply-chain logistics, while IHL tracks software expenditure and operational return in grocery, apparel, and general merchandise. Adoption is measured rather than guessed, and the Census series updates often enough to show change.

For AI specifically, the volume use cases are demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation. These run across many stores and transactions, so even small changes in adoption or software spend can signal where inference workloads are growing. But the data stops at adoption and spend. None of the four sources reports electricity demand, data center capacity, or compute requirements, so the data cannot support claims about grid constraints or building needs for retail AI.

summary: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation are the volume use cases.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau measures AI use in retail trade directly, through its Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks and reports the answer for retail trade under NAICS 44-45. The latest figure is 16.5%, against a prior period of 15.5%. The series was first asked in September 2023 and is updated fortnightly, which makes it the closest thing this sector has to a running adoption count rather than a vendor estimate.

What that use consists of is tracked by the trade bodies and research firms. The National Retail Federation covers store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software, and its account of conversations in Paris describes retailers working on practical AI, connected stores, and relationship-driven loyalty. Coresight Research produces adoption rates and market sizing for AI in merchandising and supply-chain logistics, and runs an invite-only forum on AI for consumer-focused businesses. IHL Group tracks retail technology expenditure and operational return across grocery, apparel, and general merchandise. The broad shape is demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation at volume.

IHL Group's findings point at where the money goes wrong as much as where it goes. Its 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, done in cooperation with Chain Store Age, concludes that inventory data accuracy, not AI budget size, separates specialty retail winners from laggards, and a separate IHL finding holds that most retail AI budgets fund the wrong layer first, with pilots stalling before they reach the store floor. IHL also reports inventory distortion down to $1.7 trillion, while empty shelves still cost $690.9 billion. Vendor activity on the same page runs across media, hiring, and service: Albertsons Media Collective launched Retail Media Incrementality-Based Multi-Touch Attribution with LiveRamp, linking exposure data across owned channels, Meta, offsite media and third-party inventory to Albertsons transaction data, and expanded Criteo-powered AI search and YouTube branded-content advertising. Amazon Web Services launched Amazon Connect Talent, an agentic AI hiring platform that automates high-volume recruiting. Crocs replaced scripted self-service with Rivet, a Salesforce Agentforce-powered conversational AI assistant unifying product discovery, customer support and order tracking, with plans to extend it to HEYDUDE and multilingual international markets.

Demand-side evidence on the same page comes from Acosta Group, which found that 34% of shoppers use AI tools for shopping, led by ChatGPT and Google Gemini, and that 25% routinely use Gemini for product searches. Gen Z and millennials drive that adoption, using AI for comparisons, research and in-store decisions, though only 22% trust agents to purchase autonomously. That last number is the clearest limit the sources report on how far automation can be pushed into the transaction itself.

On risk and regulation these sources say little. The regulatory posture is not set out in the material here, and the closest thing to a caution is operational rather than legal: Coresight's Shoptalk agenda has Claire's and The Children's Place checking AI against the store, and IHL's finding that pilots stall before reaching the store floor. Albertsons describes its attribution tool as privacy-enabled, which is the only privacy framing present.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a few things. Adoption is real but not universal, at 16.5% of retail firms per the Census Bureau. The reported differentiator is data quality underneath the AI, not the size of the AI budget, per IHL Group. Consumer willingness runs ahead of consumer trust, with 34% using AI tools for shopping and only 22% trusting agents to purchase autonomously, per Acosta Group. And the deployments that get described in detail, at Crocs, Albertsons and Amazon Web Services, are aimed at service, media measurement and hiring rather than at the shelf.

https://nrf.com/.brief: The National Retail Federation describes itself as an advocate for the people, policies, and ideas that support a thriving retail sector, and it provides retail news, insights, and industry events. According to the organization, conversations held in Paris illustrated how retailers are putting what it calls "The Next Now" into practice. These efforts span practical artificial intelligence, connected stores, and loyalty programs built on relationships.

https://coresight.com/.brief: Coresight Research describes itself as delivering data-driven insights on retail and technology, and claims a depth of expertise in China that it calls "unique in the industry." Its page also promotes a Shoptalk Fall 2026 Day 3 morning line-up, listing sessions on David's Bridal and Equinox selling past the core product, Crocs and Kenneth Cole marketing through entertainment, and Claire's and The Children's Place checking AI against the store. Coresight adds that it leads an invite-only yet collaborative forum exploring AI and the opportunities and challenges it presents for consumer-focused businesses.

https://ihlservices.com/.brief: IHL Group conducts research on retail technology spending and strategy. According to their 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, inventory data accuracy rather than AI budget size determines which specialty retailers succeed, and most retail AI budgets fund the wrong infrastructure layer first. The organisation also reports that inventory distortion has declined to $1.7 trillion, though empty shelves still cost $690.9 billion annually. IHL's analysis finds that the presence of AI does not predict pricing-platform quality among vendors, and retailers should instead evaluate explainability, automation controls, and governance safeguards.
